title: Stored energy: how energy waits in a twist, a height, food and a cell

summary.text: Wind up a toy, and it moves later, after you have let go. In between, the energy waits in the toy. This is called stored energy. Energy can wait in the shape of a thing, such as a twisted rubber band or a coiled clock spring. It can wait in height, such as water in the tank on the roof. And it waits in food, fuel and cells, in how their tiny particles are joined. A store can give its energy back all at once, like a jumping toy, or slowly, like a clock that ticks for a week.
summary.art: A clear plastic jar lying on a kitchen floor with a twisted rubber band and a small padlock inside it, next to a wall clock with a winding key, a tank on a roof, a banana and an AA cell.

intro.hook: Roll a jar away from you along the floor and let go. It slows down and stops. Then, with nobody touching it, it rolls back to you. What made it come back?
intro.text: The jar has a rubber band and a small weight inside. Rolling the jar away twisted the band. The twist held energy, and the energy brought the jar back. In this unit you build this roll-back jar and find out how many turns make it come back furthest. You also test a torch cell that seems finished, read the energy on food packets, and find energy waiting all over your home.
intro.art: A child kneeling on a tiled floor with arms open, and a clear jar rolling back towards them by itself, with a twisted rubber band and a padlock visible inside.

outcomes: I can say what stored energy is, and give examples of energy waiting in height, in a stretched, squashed or twisted shape, in food and fuel, and in cells.
I can build a roll-back jar, test how the number of turns changes how far it rolls back, and explain the result with what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that a store gives its energy back later, quickly or slowly, and that some of it always spreads out as warmth and sound.
I can explain why water or a ball held higher has more energy waiting, using the tank on the roof and a dam as examples.
I can explain where the energy in food comes from, and read the energy number on a food packet.
I can explain what a cell stores, why a tired cell may still run a clock, and how to handle cells safely.
I can tell how Robert Mayer's idea about food and body heat was tested, and what wrong idea it replaced.

terms.meaning: What makes things move, light up, heat up or make a sound.
terms.example: A ceiling fan needs energy from electricity to turn.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning, a torch shining and a pressure cooker whistling, in one kitchen.

terms.meaning: Energy that is waiting in a thing, ready to come out later.
terms.example: A wound-up toy car holds stored energy until you let go of it.
terms.art: A child's hand holding a wound-up toy car still on the floor, its wheels not yet moving.

terms.meaning: The scientists' name for stored energy. Potential means 'able to happen later'.
terms.example: Water in the tank on the roof has potential energy. It comes out when you open the tap downstairs.
terms.art: A water tank on the roof of a flat building with a pipe running down to a tap in a kitchen.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is moving. Scientists call it kinetic energy.
terms.example: A rolling ball has movement energy. A faster ball has more.
terms.art: A cricket ball rolling fast across a floor, with short lines behind it to show movement.

terms.meaning: Able to spring back to its shape after being stretched, squashed, bent or twisted.
terms.example: A rubber band is elastic. Let go of a stretched band and it snaps back.
terms.art: A rubber band stretched between two fingers, and then snapping back to a small loop.

terms.meaning: Turning one end of a thing while the other end stays still.
terms.example: Wringing out a wet towel twists it.
terms.art: Two hands wringing out a wet towel over a bucket, the towel twisted like a rope.

terms.meaning: A coil of springy metal that stores energy when it is squashed, stretched or wound up.
terms.example: A wind-up wall clock has a flat coiled spring inside. Winding the key coils it tighter.
terms.art: A flat steel spring coiled like a snail shell, inside an opened clock.

terms.meaning: Energy stored in how the tiny particles of a material are joined together. It comes out when the material changes, for example when it burns or is digested.
terms.example: Food, LPG gas, candle wax and the chemicals in a cell all hold chemical energy.
terms.art: A blue gas flame under a pan, a plate of idli, a candle and an AA cell side by side.

terms.meaning: A material that is burned to give out its stored energy as heat and light.
terms.example: LPG in the kitchen cylinder is a fuel. So are wood, coal, kerosene and petrol.
terms.art: A red LPG cylinder joined by a pipe to a gas stove with a blue flame.

terms.meaning: A small store of chemical energy that pushes electricity round a circuit. People often call it a battery.
terms.example: A TV remote has two AA cells inside.
terms.art: A TV remote with its back open and two AA cells inside.

terms.meaning: Strictly, two or more cells joined together. A rechargeable battery can be filled with energy again from the wall socket.
terms.example: A phone battery is charged at night and runs down during the day.
terms.art: A phone on a charger, with a battery symbol filling up on its screen.

terms.meaning: A unit for measuring how much energy is stored in food. Packets often print it as kcal, or just as Calories.
terms.example: A packet of glucose biscuits says about 450 kcal for every 100 grams.
terms.art: The back of a biscuit packet with the energy line, 'Energy 450 kcal per 100 g', circled.

terms.meaning: To let stored energy come out, for example by letting go of a stretched band.
terms.example: Opening the tap releases the water stored up in the tank.
terms.art: A hand turning a steel tap and water pouring into a steel bucket.

explanations.context: This card says what stored energy is, and why scientists also call it potential energy.
explanations.definition: Stored energy is energy that waits in a thing, because of its height, its shape or what it is made of, until it is released. Scientists call it potential energy.
explanations.description: Energy is what makes things move, light up, heat up or make a sound. Some energy is busy, like the energy of a rolling ball. Some energy is waiting. A rubber band that you hold stretched is still, but let go and it flies. Water in the tank on your roof is still, but open a tap downstairs and it rushes out. The energy was there the whole time, waiting. In 1853 a Scottish engineer, William Rankine, gave this waiting energy the name potential energy. Potential means 'able to happen later'. You cannot see stored energy. You can only see what it does when it comes out.
examples: A stretched rubber band on your fingers holds stored energy until you let go.
A coconut high on a tree holds stored energy. If the coconut falls, that energy becomes movement.
A packet of rice in the kitchen holds stored energy that your body can use after you eat it.
explanations.art: Four still things, each with a small dotted glow: a stretched rubber band on fingers, a coconut high on a tree, a water tank on a roof and a packet of rice.

explanations.concept: Energy waiting in a shape: stretch, squash, bend and twist
explanations.context: Remember the roll-back jar, where a twisted rubber band rolled the jar back? This card explains where that energy was.
explanations.definition: An elastic thing stores energy when it is stretched, squashed, bent or twisted. It gives the energy back as it springs back to its shape.
explanations.description: To twist the band inside the roll-back jar, you had to push the jar along the floor. Your push put energy into the band. The twisted band held that energy, as long as the jar stayed still. When you let go, the band untwisted and turned the jar back. The more turns you wound, the more energy the band held, and the further the jar rolled. A bow, a catapult, a trampoline and the spring inside a wind-up clock all work the same way. Something pushes or pulls to change the shape. The shape holds the energy. The energy comes back out as the thing springs back.
examples: An archer pulls back the string of a bow. The bent bow stores energy and gives it to the arrow.
A wind-up clock's key coils a flat steel spring tighter. The spring then unwinds slowly and turns the clock's wheels.
A mattress squashes when you jump on it, then pushes you back up.
explanations.art: A row of four drawings: a bent bow with an arrow, a coiled clock spring, a squashed mattress and a twisted rubber band inside a jar.

explanations.context: This card is about why things held higher have more energy waiting, from a coconut to the water tank on your roof.
explanations.definition: When you lift a thing against the Earth's pull, called gravity, you store energy. The higher and heavier the thing, the more energy is stored. It comes out as movement when the thing falls.
explanations.description: Gravity is the pull of the Earth on everything. To lift a water bottle onto a high shelf, your arm works against gravity, and that work is stored. If the bottle falls, the stored energy turns into movement, and it lands with a thud. A bottle on a higher shelf would land harder, because more energy was stored. This is why many buildings in Indian cities have a water tank on the roof. A motor pumps water up into the tank once or twice a day. Then the water stays there, high up, with energy waiting. When anyone opens a tap, the water rushes down the pipes by itself. Taps on the ground floor usually flow harder than taps on the top floor, because the water above them has fallen further. Scientists say the stored energy belongs to the bottle and the Earth together, because the Earth's pull is what makes the fall.
examples: Hydroelectric power stations, such as the one at the Mettur dam on the Kaveri river, let water stored high behind a dam fall through pipes to spin machines that make electricity.
A child at the top of a slide has stored energy that becomes speed on the way down.
A coconut high on a palm tree has much more energy waiting than one on a low branch.
explanations.art: A tall flat building with a water tank on its roof, a motor pumping water up, and pipes running down to taps on each floor, with the ground-floor tap flowing hardest.

explanations.concept: Energy waiting in food and fuel
explanations.context: This card is about chemical energy: the energy stored in food, gas, wood and wax.
explanations.definition: Chemical energy is stored in how the tiny particles of a material are joined. When food is digested, or a fuel burns, the particles join up in new ways and the energy comes out.
explanations.description: Everything is made of tiny particles called atoms, joined into groups called molecules. In food and fuel, the atoms are joined in a way that holds energy. When gas burns on the stove, it joins with oxygen from the air, and the energy comes out quickly as heat and light. Your body does almost the same thing with food, but slowly and in many small steps. It joins the food with oxygen from your breath, and the energy comes out as warmth and as the movement of your muscles. That is why you breathe faster when you run. The energy in almost all food was first caught from sunlight by plants. A plant uses sunlight to build sugar from air and water, and the sugar holds the energy. Oils and fats hold the most energy for their weight. Sugar, rice and dal hold less than half as much, and fresh fruit much less, because fruit is mostly water.
examples: 100 grams of cooking oil holds about 900 kcal. 100 grams of banana holds only about 90 kcal, because a banana is mostly water.
A camel crosses deserts where food can be hard to find for days. Their hump is a store of fat, and their body uses it for energy when there is little to eat.
A candle burns its wax, and the wax's stored energy comes out as light and heat.
explanations.art: A plate with a dosa and a banana on a steel table, a bottle of groundnut oil, and a gas flame, with small labels showing which holds the most energy for its weight.

explanations.concept: Energy waiting in cells and batteries
explanations.context: This card is about what a cell stores, and why a cell that is too tired for a torch can still run a clock.
explanations.definition: A cell stores chemical energy. When it is joined into a circuit, its chemicals slowly react, and the energy comes out as a push on electricity.
explanations.description: Inside an AA cell are two different chemicals, kept apart. When the cell is in a torch and the switch is on, the chemicals react, a little at a time, and push electricity round the circuit. As the chemicals get used, the push gets weaker. A torch bulb needs a big flow of electricity, so a tired cell makes it dim. A wall clock needs only a tiny trickle, so the same tired cell can often run a clock for weeks more. A phone has a rechargeable battery. Charging uses electricity from the wall to push its chemicals back the way they were, so the energy is stored again. An ordinary AA cell must never be charged, because it can leak, get hot or burst.
examples: An AA cell that has stopped lighting a torch brightly may still keep a wall clock ticking.
An inverter at home charges big batteries while the power is on. In a power cut, the batteries run the fans and lights.
An electric scooter is charged overnight, and the stored energy turns its wheels during the day.
explanations.art: A dim torch next to a ticking wall clock, with the same AA cell shown going from the torch into the clock.

explanations.concept: A store lets energy come out later, quickly or slowly
explanations.context: Remember the wait test, when you held the wound jar still for a minute before letting go? This card explains what that showed.
explanations.definition: A store keeps energy until it is released. It can release the energy all at once or a little at a time.
explanations.description: When you held the wound jar still for a minute, nothing moved, but the jar still rolled back when you let go. Your push had ended a minute earlier. The energy waited in the band in between. This is what makes stores so useful. Ammamma winds a clock for a few minutes on a Sunday, and the spring lets the energy out a tiny bit at each tick, for eight days. A bow stores energy slowly, as the archer pulls, and gives it all to the arrow in a moment. A flea needs to jump onto a dog many times their own height. Their leg muscles are too slow to throw them that high. So the flea slowly squeezes a pad of very springy material in their body, called resilin, then lets it go all at once.
examples: A pendulum wall clock wound once a week keeps ticking all week.
A flea stores energy slowly in a springy pad, then jumps in about a thousandth of a second.
A phone is charged for two hours at night and uses the energy slowly all day.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a grandmother winding a wall clock with a key on a Sunday, and a calendar showing the clock still ticking on Saturday.

explanations.context: Your roll-back jar never came back quite as far as you hoped, and it stopped in the end. This card explains why.
explanations.definition: When stored energy comes out, all of it goes somewhere, but some always spreads out as a little warmth and sound that we cannot get back.
explanations.description: Energy is never made from nothing, and it never vanishes. So a store can give back at most the energy that was put in. In real life it gives back less, because some energy always spreads out. As the roll-back jar rolls, it rubs on the floor and makes a soft rumbling sound. The band rubs inside itself as it twists and untwists, and gets very slightly warm. That warmth and sound are still energy, but they spread into the air and the floor, and nobody can collect them again. So the jar rolls back and forth a few times, each time a little less, and then stops.
examples: A bouncing ball bounces lower each time, and stops in the end.
Stretch and let go of a thick rubber band ten times quickly, then touch it to your lip. It feels slightly warm.
A swing slows down unless someone keeps pushing.
explanations.art: A roll-back jar's path drawn as a line going back and forth on a floor, each swing shorter, with tiny sound marks and wavy warmth lines.

explanations.context: This card is about how plants and animals store energy for later, each for their own life.
explanations.definition: Living things store energy, as food or in springy body parts, to use when they need it.
explanations.description: A seed must grow a root and a shoot in the dark soil, before they can catch any sunlight. So their parent plant packs food into them, as starch or oil, and the seed lives on that food until their first leaves open. A groundnut seed is full of oil for this reason. A bear in a cold country sleeps through the winter, when there is little food. So they eat a lot in autumn and store it as fat. Your own body stores some energy as a sugar called glycogen in your muscles and liver, and much more as fat. That is how you can run in the evening on energy from your lunch.
examples: A groundnut seed is about half oil, stored by their parent plant to feed the young plant.
A camel's hump is fat, used for energy on long trips with little food.
Your muscles store a little sugar, ready for a sudden run.
explanations.art: A groundnut split open beside a young groundnut seedling, a camel walking across sand, and a child running, each with a small glowing store drawn in.

explanations.context: This card is about a question that scientists still argue about: what energy actually is.
explanations.description: Scientists can measure energy very exactly, and the numbers always add up. But they do not agree on what energy is. When it is stored, you cannot see it, weigh it or touch it. The physicist Richard Feynman said in his lectures in the 1960s that in physics today we have no knowledge of what energy is. He meant that we know its rules, but not what it is made of.
examples: A stretched band and a loose band look almost the same, but one holds energy and one does not.
Physicists can calculate exactly how far a ball will bounce, without knowing what energy is.

perspectives.explanation: Energy is a number we calculate. It always comes out the same before and after any change, so it is very useful. It is not a stuff that sits inside things.
Energy is real. Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy are the same thing in two forms, so energy is part of what everything is made of.
Energy may be the ability of the world to change. A store is a change that has not happened yet.

explanations.art: A child holding a stretched rubber band and looking at it closely with a magnifying glass, with a question mark drawn above.

agreed.text: Energy can be stored in a thing's height, its shape, or the chemicals it is made of, and released later.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can wind a toy, lift a ball or eat a meal and see the energy come out later. Scientists measure these stores very exactly.

agreed.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. It only changes from one form to another.
agreed.evidence: In every careful experiment since the 1840s, the energy before a change has added up to the energy after it, once warmth and sound are counted.

agreed.text: The energy in food is chemical energy, and almost all of it came first from sunlight caught by plants.
agreed.evidence: Plants grown in the dark use up their seed's food and stop growing. Measurements show that burning food gives out the same energy as the body gets from it.

agreed.text: When stored energy comes out, some always spreads out as warmth and sound.
agreed.evidence: No bouncing ball, swing or wound toy keeps going for ever. Careful thermometers show the warming.

challenging.claim: A thing that is not moving has no energy.
challenging.who: A very common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: We see energy when something moves, lights up or makes a sound. A still thing seems to be doing nothing.
challenging.against: A wound jar held still, a coconut high on a tree and a packet of food are all still, yet they all hold energy that comes out later.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only moving things have energy.

challenging.claim: The energy of a raised ball is stored in the ball alone.
challenging.who: How most people, and many books, say it
challenging.for: It is easier to say, and the ball is the thing that moves when it falls.
challenging.against: Physicists say the stored energy belongs to the ball and the Earth together, because it comes from the pull between them. Far from the Earth, lifting the ball would store almost nothing.
challenging.context: This card is about where the energy of a raised ball really is.

challenging.claim: Living bodies make their heat with a special life force, not from their food.
challenging.for: A living body stays warm and moves by itself, while a dead one goes cold. It seemed something special to life was at work.
challenging.against: Robert Mayer said the warmth and movement come from the energy in food. In the 1890s Max Rubner measured all the heat given out by dogs, and it matched the energy in the food they used.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where body heat comes from.

challenging.claim: The kcal number on a packet tells you how good a food is for you.
challenging.for: Eating much more energy than you use, for years, can make a body store too much fat.
challenging.against: A kcal number says only how much energy is stored. It says nothing about protein, vitamins or fibre. Groundnuts are high in kcal and full of protein. A sweet drink is lower and has almost nothing else.
challenging.context: This card is about what the energy number on a food packet does and does not tell you.

challenging.claim: A cell that will not light a torch is completely empty.
challenging.for: The torch stays dark, so it seems all the energy has gone.
challenging.against: A tired cell still holds some energy, but it can push only a small flow of electricity. A wall clock needs only a tiny flow, so the cell can often still run it.
challenging.context: This card is about cells that seem to be finished.

big_questions.q: Your push ended a minute before the jar rolled back. Is the rolling caused by the push, or by the band?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen with no push, and what would happen with no band.

big_questions.q: Where exactly is the energy in a twisted rubber band? In the band, in its tiny particles, or between them?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changes inside the band when it twists. Nothing is added to it.

big_questions.q: The energy in your breakfast was sunlight, caught by a plant. Is part of you made of stored sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your body builds from food, as well as what it burns.

big_questions.q: A seed can wait in a dry packet for years, then grow when it is watered. Is a seed alive while they wait?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a seed is doing in the packet, and what they need to start growing.

big_questions.q: If a still thing can hold energy, how can you tell whether anything is truly at rest?
big_questions.hint: Think of the tank on the roof and the coconut on the tree. What would you need to know about them?

big_questions.q: Coal and petrol are stores of energy from plants and sea creatures that lived millions of years ago. Should we use up stores that took so long to make?
big_questions.hint: Think about who made the store, how long it took, and who else might need it.

story.title: Ammamma's Clock
story.note: The story is made up. Everything about the clock is true: many old pendulum wall clocks are 'eight-day clocks', wound with a key once a week, and the key coils a flat steel spring that turns the clock's wheels.
text: In Nikhil's flat in Mysuru, the loudest thing in the hall was the clock. It hung high on the wall, in a wooden case with a glass door. Behind the glass, a brass pendulum swung left and right, left and right. Tick, tock. Tick, tock. Every hour it struck the time with deep, round bongs. The clock had belonged to Ammamma's father, and it was older than anyone in the family.
That month, Ammamma went to Chennai for her niece's wedding. She was away for ten days. Nikhil was eight, and he liked having the hall to himself. He did his sums to the tick-tock of the clock.

On the ninth morning, something was wrong. Nikhil sat down with his tumbler of milk and listened. The hall was silent. The pendulum hung straight down, perfectly still. The hands said twenty past four, though it was seven o'clock.
"Amma! Divya! The clock is broken," he shouted.
His big sister Divya came to look. She tapped the glass. Nothing. "Maybe it got too old," she said. "Maybe it is just tired."
Their mother looked up at the clock and smiled. "Wait for Ammamma," she said. "She comes back tomorrow."
The next evening Ammamma came home with a bag of sweets and a jasmine string in her hair. Before she had even had her coffee, Nikhil pulled her into the hall. "Ammamma, your clock has died."
Ammamma looked at the still pendulum. "It has not died, kanna. It is hungry." She opened the little brass box on the shelf below the clock. Inside lay a key, shaped like a small T.
She stood on a stool and opened the glass door. There were two holes in the clock's face. She fitted the key into one and began to turn it. Click, click, click. "Count for me," she said.
Nikhil counted. After about ten turns, the key would not go round any more.

"Now feel this," said Ammamma. She let Nikhil put his fingers on the key and try to turn it one more time. It pushed back against his fingers, hard. "Inside, there is a long, flat strip of steel, coiled up like a snail shell," Ammamma said. "Every turn of the key winds it tighter. Now it is wound right up. It is pushing, all the time, to unwind."
"Then why doesn't it unwind all at once?" asked Nikhil.

Ammamma touched the pendulum gently, and it began to swing. Tick, tock. The clock was alive again. "Because of this," she said. "Each time the pendulum swings, it lets one tooth of a little wheel go past. So the spring can only turn the wheels one tooth at a time, one tick at a time. A few minutes of winding is let out slowly, over eight days. That is why my father called it an eight-day clock. And that is why I wind it every Sunday."
Nikhil thought about this. "But you were away for ten days."
"So it ran for eight, and on the ninth morning the spring had nothing left to give." Ammamma climbed down from the stool. "Nothing in it was broken. Nobody had put energy into it."
Divya laughed. "So it was tired, after all."
"In a way," said Ammamma. "But a clock does not rest and get better. It only gets back what someone gives it."
Nikhil was still looking at the key. "So the ticking on Thursday came from your arm on Sunday?"
Ammamma smiled. "From my arm, from my breakfast, and from the sun that grew the ragi in my breakfast. All of it waiting in that spring."

That night, Nikhil lay in bed and listened to the clock. Tick, tock. He thought of the strip of steel, coiled tight in the dark, giving out a tiny bit of Sunday with every swing. The next Sunday, before anyone else was up, he stood on the stool and asked Ammamma to show him again. This time, he turned the key himself.
story.epiphany: The ticking of a whole week was put into the clock in a few minutes of winding. The energy waited in the spring and came out a tiny bit at each tick.
ask: Why had the clock stopped? Was anything broken?
Ammamma wound the clock for a few minutes. How long did that energy last?
Where did the energy in the spring come from, before Ammamma's arm?
Can you think of something at home that stores energy quickly and lets it out slowly?

The boy lying in bed at night, listening, with a drawing of a coiled steel spring floating above him like a thought.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Bonus points for naming the store

rules: Lay the 4 store cards face up in a row. Shuffle the picture cards and put them face down.
On your turn, turn over a picture card and say 'waiting' or 'moving'.
If you are right, you win the card. If the energy is waiting, put it under the right store card and say what would let the energy out. That earns a bonus point.
If you are wrong, the card goes to the bottom of the pile.
When all the cards are won, the player with the most cards and bonus points wins. Playing alone, try to win 20 cards with no more than 4 mistakes.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Lay the 4 store cards in a row. 3. Shuffle the picture cards.
flow.say: Each card shows something with energy. You say whether its energy is waiting or moving.
flow.kid: Each card has energy. Is it waiting or moving? Say which!
flow.context: This is the first step of Waiting or Moving, a card game about stored energy.

flow.do: Take turns turning over cards, saying waiting or moving, and placing waiting cards under a store.
flow.say: A coconut on the tree. Waiting or moving? Which store? What would let its energy out?
flow.kid: Turn a card. Waiting or moving? Which store? How does the energy come out?
flow.parent: The tricky cards are the phone on charge and the clock key being turned. Their energy is moving into a store, filling it. Accept either answer if your child explains it.

check.q: Which card shows energy waiting in height?

A water tank on the roof
A plate of idli
check.why: Water in a tank on the roof is high up, so energy waits in its height. It comes out when a tap is opened. The racing car's energy is moving. The idli stores food energy, not height.

A bird toy: flap your arms

rules: One player is the Winder. Everyone else picks a toy card and freezes.
The Winder turns an invisible key on a player's back, counting the turns out loud, from 1 to 10.
The player must stay frozen until the Winder says 'Let go!'
Then the player acts out their toy: 1 turn gives 1 step, 5 turns give 5 steps. They slow down as they run out, and stop.
A player who moves before 'Let go!' or does more steps than turns becomes the next Winder.

flow.do: Explain the rules, and give each player a toy card.
flow.say: I am the Winder. I'll wind you with a key. You stay frozen until I say let go. Then you move one step for every turn.
flow.kid: Pick a toy card. Freeze. Wait to be wound up!
flow.context: This is the first step of Wind Me Up, an acting game about stored energy.

flow.do: Play several rounds. Sometimes wait a long time before saying 'Let go!'
flow.say: Three turns. Now wait. Wait. Let go! How many steps did you have?
flow.kid: Stay frozen while you wait. When you hear 'Let go!', take your steps. Slow down at the end.
flow.parent: The long waits are the point. The energy was put in by the winding, and it waits until it is let go.

flow.do: Ask what the game showed.
flow.say: When I wound you and made you wait, where was your energy while you were frozen?
flow.kid: While you were frozen, where was your energy?

check.q: Gowri was wound 4 turns and had to wait. When she was let go, how many steps should she take?
options: More than 4, because she rested
4 steps, the same as her winding
None, because waiting used her energy up
check.why: A store gives back what was put in, so 4 turns gives 4 steps. Waiting does not add energy. A real spring loses only a tiny bit while it waits.

setup.art: A woman turning an invisible key on the back of a frozen child pretending to be a robot, in a living room.
setup.caption: 1. The Winder winds a frozen toy.

setup.art: The child marching stiffly forward like a robot, slowing down, with step marks on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Let go! One step for each turn.

experiments.title: The Roll-Back Jar: do more turns make it roll back further?
experiments.context: In this experiment you build a jar that rolls back to you by itself. Then you test whether winding it more turns makes it roll back further, and whether the energy waits while you hold it still.
experiments.question: Does winding the roll-back jar more turns make it roll back further? And does the energy stay in it if you hold it still for a minute?
experiments.predict: We will wind the jar 1, 2, 3 and 4 turns. Guess how far it will roll back each time. Will 4 turns go further than 1 turn, the same, or less? And if we hold it still for a minute before letting go, will it still roll back? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same jar, the same band, the same padlock and the same floor every time. Roll the jar slowly by hand, and let go without pushing. Only the number of turns changes. Try each number of turns 3 times and use the middle result, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a round plastic jar with a lid, about 8 to 12 cm wide and 10 to 15 cm long, such as an empty malt-drink, peanut butter or dry-fruit jar. A clear jar lets you see the band twist.
rubber bands, looped together into a chain a little shorter than the jar
a small weight: a small padlock, a heavy steel nut, or 6 one-rupee coins taped into a stack
a piece of thread about 15 cm long
two halves of a used matchstick or a toothpick
cello tape and a strip of coloured tape or a marker
a nail or the point of a pair of scissors, for a grown-up to make two holes
a tailor's measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler, and a piece of chalk or a sticky note to mark the floor
a clear, flat floor about 3 metres long, such as a hall or a corridor

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the holes in the lid and the base, because the nail or scissor point can slip. Keep fingers away from the point. If a rubber band snaps, it can sting, so keep your face away from a tight band.

schedule.what: Build the roll-back jar. Guess, then test 1, 2, 3 and 4 turns, 3 tries each. Do the wait test. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each number of turns, as tall as the middle result. Write one sentence under it: what the bars show.

flow.do: 1. Roll an empty jar with its lid on along the floor towards your child. 2. Ask what they notice. 3. Then show the jar with the band and padlock inside, before you build it.
flow.say: Watch this empty jar. I roll it, and it keeps going until it stops. Now we will make a jar that comes back to you by itself.
flow.kid: Roll an empty jar along the floor. It goes away and stops. Now let's make one that comes back!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Roll-Back Jar experiment. You see an ordinary jar roll, before building one that rolls back.

flow.do: 1. Make a small hole in the centre of the lid and the centre of the base. 2. Loop three bands into a chain. 3. Push one end through the base hole and slip half a matchstick through the loop outside. Tape it down. 4. Tie the padlock to the middle of the band chain with thread, so it hangs about 1 cm below. 5. Pull the other end through the lid hole, fix it with the other matchstick, and close the lid.
flow.say: I'll make the holes, because the nail can slip. You loop the bands together and tie the padlock to the middle. The padlock must hang down without touching the side of the jar.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes the holes. You loop the bands. Tie the padlock to the middle. It must hang down, not touch the side.
flow.parent: The band should run straight from the middle of the base to the middle of the lid, a little stretched. If the padlock touches the side of the jar, shorten the thread or the band chain. Stick a strip of coloured tape along the outside of the jar, so you can count the turns as it rolls.

flow.do: 1. Put the jar on its side on a chalk line on the floor. 2. Ask your child to guess how far it will roll back after 1, 2, 3 and 4 turns. 3. Write each guess in the table. 4. Ask the second question: will it still roll back if we hold it still for a minute?
flow.say: When I roll this jar forward, what do you think happens to the band inside? How far will it roll back after one turn? After four turns? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how far it rolls back after 1, 2, 3 and 4 turns. Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why do you think more turns will make it roll back further?
good: Because the band gets more twisted.
Because more twisting stores more energy.

flow.parent: Do not explain yet. Any guess is good if your child gives a reason. Some children think it will roll back the same however far it goes. That is a fine guess to test.

flow.do: 1. Hold the jar on the chalk line with the tape strip on top. 2. Roll it forward slowly with your palm, exactly 1 turn, counting by the tape. 3. Hold it still, then lift your hand without pushing. 4. Mark where it first stops. 5. Measure from where you let go to that mark. 6. Repeat 3 times, then do 2, 3 and 4 turns.
flow.say: Roll it slowly, and count the turns by the tape. Now lift your hand without pushing. Where does it stop first? Let's measure from where you let go.
flow.kid: Roll the jar 1 turn. Let go gently. Where does it stop? Measure. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: Each turn twists the band one more turn, because the padlock stays hanging at the bottom. The jar usually rolls back past the chalk line, slows down, and may wobble back again. Measure only to the place where it first stops. Expect more turns to send it further, for example about 40 cm for 1 turn and over 1 metre for 4 turns. A 10 cm wide jar rolls about 30 cm in each turn, so 4 turns needs about 1.3 metres of floor in front, and the same behind. If the padlock swings right over the band inside and the band unwinds without moving the jar, the band is too strong for the weight. Use a heavier weight or fewer turns.

check.q: Leela, a girl in Class 3, winds her roll-back jar 1 turn, then 4 turns. What did your own test show will happen?
options: It rolls back the same distance both times
It rolls back further after 4 turns
It rolls back further after 1 turn
check.why: More turns twist the band more, so it holds more energy, and the jar rolls back further. If your own results did not show this, check that you let go gently without pushing, and that the padlock does not rub the side of the jar.

flow.do: 1. Wind the jar 3 turns again. 2. Hold it still on the floor while you both count slowly to 60. 3. Let go gently. 4. Measure, and compare with your 3-turn results.
flow.say: This time, wind 3 turns and hold it still. Let's count to 60 together. Is anything moving? Now let go. Did it still come back?
flow.kid: Wind 3 turns. Hold it still. Count to 60. Nothing moves. Now let go!
flow.parent: The jar should roll back about as far as your other 3-turn tries, perhaps a little less. While it was held still, the energy waited in the twisted band. This wait test is the heart of the unit, so let your child say what they notice before you say anything.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: more turns make the jar roll back further, and the energy waits in the band. What I saw: 1 turn went about 40 cm, 4 turns went over a metre. After holding it still for a minute, it still came back. Why: rolling the jar twists the band, and the twist stores energy. The more twists, the more energy waits in it.

check.q: In the wait test, the jar was held still for a minute and then rolled back. Where was the energy during that minute?
options: In the padlock
In the twisted rubber band
It had gone, and came back from the floor
check.why: The energy waited in the twisted rubber band. The padlock only holds the middle of the band still, so that rolling the jar twists it. Picking 'the floor' is a fair guess, because the floor helps the jar roll, but the floor was the same before and after. The band was the thing that was twisted.

setup.caption: 1. Gather the jar, bands, a padlock and two matchstick halves.

setup.art: A cut-away drawing of the jar on its side, with the rubber band running from the centre of the base to the centre of the lid, held outside by matchstick halves, and the padlock tied to the middle of the band, hanging just below it.
setup.caption: 2. Thread the band through, and tie the padlock to its middle.

setup.art: A child's hand rolling the jar slowly forward along a tiled floor, with a strip of coloured tape on the jar to count the turns, and the band inside twisting.
setup.caption: 3. Roll the jar forward slowly. Count the turns.

setup.art: The jar rolling back by itself along the floor towards a chalk start line, with a tailor's tape laid beside its path.
setup.caption: 4. Let go. Measure how far it rolls back.

experiments.title: The Tired Cell: is a cell that dims a torch really empty?
experiments.context: In this experiment you take a cell that has stopped lighting a torch well, and test whether it still has energy left for a wall clock.
experiments.question: Does an AA cell that makes a torch dim still have energy that can run a wall clock?
experiments.predict: This cell makes the torch dim. Do you think it will run the wall clock? Will the clock tick, tick slowly, or stay still? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same torch and the same clock for every cell. Test a fresh cell too, so you can compare. Watch the clock's second hand for a full minute each time.
results_table: Clock after 1 minute: ticking or still?
Clock next day: still on time?

materials.item: one or two AA cells that have made a torch or a toy go dim. Keep them in a box when they start to fade.
one fresh AA cell, to compare
a torch or a toy that takes AA cells
a wall clock or a table clock that runs on one AA cell
a phone or another clock, to check the time

experiments.safety: Never open, cut, heat or try to charge an ordinary cell. If a cell has a white crust or is leaking, do not use it. Wipe it with a dry cloth, put it in a bag for e-waste, and wash your hands. Keep small round button cells away from babies, because a swallowed button cell can badly burn a child's food pipe within two hours.

schedule.what: Test each cell in the torch. Guess, then test it in the clock. Set the clock to the right time.
Check whether the clock is still ticking and still on time. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then finish this sentence: 'A cell that is too tired for a torch...'

flow.do: 1. Put the fresh cell in the torch and switch it on. 2. Then put a tired cell in and switch it on. 3. Compare how bright the torch is.
flow.say: Here is a new cell and an old one. Let's see how each one lights the torch. Which is brighter?
flow.kid: Try the new cell in the torch. Then try the old cell. Which is brighter?
flow.parent: The tired cell should make the torch clearly dimmer, or not light it at all. If it lights the torch as brightly as the new one, it is not tired yet. Use another.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tired Cell experiment. You compare a fresh cell with a tired one in a torch.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess whether the tired cell will run the clock, and why.
flow.say: This cell can hardly light the torch. Do you think it can run the clock? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: This cell can hardly light the torch. Will it run the clock? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the clock will not work?
good: Because the torch did not light, so there is no energy left.

ask.q: Why do you think the clock might still work?
good: Because a clock needs less energy than a torch.
Because the torch was dim, not dark, so a little energy is left.

flow.parent: Both guesses are good if your child gives a reason. Do not tell them the answer.

flow.do: 1. Put the tired cell in the clock, the right way round. 2. Set the clock to the right time. 3. Watch the second hand for one full minute. 4. Write what happens.
flow.say: Put the cell in with the flat end on the spring. Now let's watch the second hand together for one whole minute.
flow.kid: Put the cell in the clock. Flat end on the spring. Watch the second hand for one minute.
flow.parent: Very often a cell that is too tired for a torch still runs a clock, sometimes for weeks. A torch bulb needs a big flow of electricity, and a clock needs only a tiny trickle. If the clock stays still, the cell is truly flat. Try your second tired cell if you have one.

flow.wait: Leave the clock running until tomorrow.
flow.do: 1. The next day, compare the clock with a phone. 2. Write whether it is still ticking and still on time.
flow.say: Is the clock still going? Is it showing the right time, like the phone?
flow.kid: Is the clock still ticking? Does it match the phone?
flow.parent: If it is still on time, the tired cell had plenty of energy left for the clock. Keep the cell in the clock and see how many more days or weeks it lasts.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a tired cell is not empty. What I saw: it made the torch dim, but the clock ticked all night. Why: the torch needs a big flow of electricity and the clock needs only a little, so the cell still had enough stored energy for the clock.

check.q: Rohini's TV remote has stopped working. Her mother says the cells are empty. What could Rohini try before throwing them away?
options: Put them in the freezer to fill them up
Try them in a wall clock, which needs only a tiny flow of electricity
Open them up to see if they are empty
check.why: A cell that is too tired for one thing may still run something that needs less, such as a wall clock. Freezing does not put energy back into a cell. Opening a cell is dangerous, because the chemicals inside can burn skin.

setup.caption: 1. Compare a new cell and a tired cell in a torch.

setup.art: A child's hand putting an AA cell into the back of a round wall clock, flat end against the spring.
setup.caption: 2. Put the tired cell in a clock.

setup.caption: 3. Watch the second hand. Check it again the next day.

activities.title: Energy Waiting: a home hunt
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find things that have energy waiting in them, ready to come out later.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Look at the gas cylinder, the stove and switches, but do not touch them. Do not climb to reach high things.

schedule.what: Hunt for 8 things with energy waiting in them, and sort them into four kinds of store.

activities.record: Draw a table with four columns: height, shape, food and fuel, cells. Write each thing you find in the right column.

flow.do: Hold a rubber band stretched between your fingers, very still. Ask your child whether the band has any energy.
flow.say: This band is not moving. Does it have any energy? What will happen when I let go?
flow.kid: The band is still. Does it have energy? Watch when I let go!
flow.parent: Let go so that the band flies away from both of you, towards a wall. Then say that the energy was waiting in the stretch.
flow.context: This is the first step of a home hunt for things with energy waiting in them.

flow.do: 1. Walk through every room together. 2. Find 8 things that have energy waiting. 3. For each, ask what would let the energy out.
flow.say: Let's find things that have energy waiting in them. For each one, tell me how we could let the energy out.
flow.kid: Find 8 things with energy waiting. How would the energy come out?

ask.q: Where is the energy waiting in the water tank on the roof?
good: In its height. When we open a tap, the water falls down the pipe.

flow.parent: Good finds are the water tank, a book on a high shelf, a wound-up toy, a hair clip or a clothes peg, a mattress, the rice tin, the gas cylinder, a candle, the TV remote, a phone, and the inverter batteries. A child at the top of the stairs counts too.

flow.do: Sort the finds into four kinds of store: height, shape, food and fuel, and cells.
flow.say: Now let's sort them. Which ones are high up? Which are stretched, squashed or twisted? Which are food or fuel? Which have cells?
flow.kid: Sort your finds. High up? Stretched or twisted? Food or fuel? Cells?

check.q: Asha, a girl in Class 3, finds a clothes peg pinching a towel on the line. What kind of store is in the peg?
options: A height store
A shape store, in its squashed spring
A food store
check.why: A clothes peg has a small metal spring that is squashed when the peg is closed on the towel. The squashed spring holds energy, and it pinches the towel. A peg on the line is a little high up too, but the pinch comes from the spring.

setup.art: A child walking through a flat holding a clipboard, pointing at a wall clock, a water tank seen through a window and a gas cylinder.
setup.caption: 1. Walk round your home and look.

setup.art: A hand-drawn table with four columns labelled height, shape, food and fuel, and cells, with small drawings in each.
setup.caption: 2. Sort your finds into four kinds of store.

activities.title: The Pop-Up Jumper
activities.context: In this activity you make a little card toy that jumps by itself a moment after you let go of it. A rubber band stores the energy.

materials.item: thin card from an empty cereal or tea box
a rubber band
scissors, cello tape and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Point the jumper away from faces when you let it go.

schedule.what: Make the jumper. Try a loose band and a tight band. See which jumps higher.

activities.record: Draw your jumper folded flat and jumping. Write which band made it jump higher.

flow.do: 1. Cut two squares of card, 8 cm by 8 cm. 2. Lay them side by side with a 2 mm gap. 3. Tape along the gap on both sides, to make a hinge. 4. Cut a small notch in the middle of each far edge. 5. Stretch the band across the back, from notch to notch.
flow.say: We are making a hinge, like the spine of a book. The band goes across the back, from one notch to the other.
flow.kid: Cut two squares. Tape them together like a book. Cut a notch on each far side. Put the band across the back.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pop-Up Jumper. You make a card hinge with a rubber band across it.

flow.do: 1. Fold the card in half with the band on the outside. 2. Press it flat on the floor with one finger. 3. Lift your finger quickly.
flow.say: Fold it so that the band goes round the outside. Press it flat. What do you feel pushing your finger? Now let go quickly.
flow.kid: Fold it with the band outside. Press it flat. Feel the push? Let go fast!
flow.parent: Folding the card with the band outside stretches the band further. The stretched band snaps the card open, and the card hits the floor and jumps. If it only opens without jumping, use a tighter band or a smaller card.

ask.q: Where was the energy while you held it flat?
good: In the band, because folding stretched it.

flow.do: 1. Try a looser band, then a tighter band. 2. See which one makes the jumper jump higher.
flow.say: Which band do you think will make it jump higher, the loose one or the tight one? Why? Let's try.
flow.kid: Try a loose band. Then a tight band. Which jumps higher? Why?

check.q: Which band made the jumper jump higher?
options: The loose band
The tight band
Both jumped the same
check.why: A tighter band is stretched more when the card is folded, so it stores more energy and throws the card higher. If both jumped about the same, the two bands may be too alike. Try a thick band and a thin one.

setup.caption: 1. Make a card hinge with a band across the back.

setup.art: A finger pressing the folded card flat on a floor, the band stretched round the outside of the fold.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it with the band outside and press it flat.

setup.art: The card springing open and leaping into the air above a floor, with movement lines.
setup.caption: 3. Let go and watch it jump.

activities.title: Energy on the Packet: which food stores the most?
activities.context: In this activity you read the energy number on food packets in your kitchen, and find which foods store the most energy for their weight.

materials.item: 4 to 6 food packets from the kitchen, such as biscuits, rice, atta, dal, sugar, cooking oil, groundnuts or a noodle packet
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Only look at the packets. Do not eat from them without asking.

schedule.what: Find the energy number on each packet. Put the foods in order, from most to least energy per 100 grams.

activities.record: Make a list of the foods, with the energy number per 100 grams next to each. Draw a star next to the one with the most.

flow.do: 1. Turn a biscuit packet over. 2. Find the table called nutrition information. 3. Find the line that says Energy, and the number with kcal next to it, per 100 g.
flow.say: Food stores energy, and the packet tells us how much. Look for the word Energy, and a number with kcal. That is the energy stored in 100 grams.
flow.kid: Turn the packet over. Find the word Energy. Find the number with kcal.
flow.parent: Kcal means kilocalories, a unit for energy in food. Some packets also give kJ, kilojoules. Use the kcal number. Use the 'per 100 g' column so all the foods are compared fairly.
flow.context: This is the first step of the food packet activity. You find the energy number on a food packet.

flow.do: 1. Before reading the other packets, ask your child to guess which food stores the most energy. 2. Then read each packet and write the number.
flow.say: Which do you think stores the most energy for its weight, the oil, the sugar or the rice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which food has the most energy? Why? Now read the packets.
flow.parent: Cooking oil is usually about 900 kcal per 100 g, the most of all. Groundnuts are about 550 to 600. Biscuits are about 450 to 500. Sugar is about 400. Rice, atta and dal are about 340 to 360. Many children guess sugar, because sugar gives a quick burst of energy.

flow.do: Put the foods in order from most to least energy, and talk about the pattern.
flow.say: The oil and the groundnuts are at the top. What do they have in common?
flow.kid: Put them in order. What do the top foods have in common?

check.q: Which kind of food stores the most energy for its weight?
options: Fats and oils
Fresh fruit
Sugar
check.why: Fats and oils store the most energy for their weight, about twice as much as sugar, rice or dal. Fresh fruit stores the least, because most of a fruit is water. Seeds like groundnuts are full of oil, packed in by their parent plant to feed the young plant.

setup.caption: 1. Gather some food packets.

setup.art: A close-up of the nutrition table on the back of a packet with the line 'Energy (kcal) per 100 g' circled in pencil.

activities.title: Three Holes in a Bottle: why the tank is on the roof
activities.context: In this activity you make three holes in a bottle, one above the other, and see which jet of water shoots out hardest. It shows why water stored high up has energy waiting.

materials.item: an empty 1 or 2 litre plastic bottle
a nail or a thick needle, for a grown-up to make the holes
cello tape
a bucket or a large tray, and a jug of water
an upturned steel bowl or a brick, to stand the bottle on

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes, because the nail can slip. Do this in the bathroom or on the balcony, where splashes do not matter.

schedule.what: Make three holes in a bottle. Guess which jet will shoot out hardest. Fill it and watch.

activities.record: Draw the bottle and the three jets, as they really came out. Write which jet was strongest, and why.

flow.do: 1. Make three holes in a line up the side of the bottle. 2. Put one 3 cm from the bottom, one in the middle and one near the top. 3. Cover all three with one strip of tape.
flow.say: I'll make three holes, one above the other. We'll cover them with tape until we are ready.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes three holes, one above the other. Cover them with tape.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Three Holes activity. You make holes at three heights in a bottle.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bottle on the upturned bowl in the bucket. 2. Fill it to the top with water. 3. Ask your child to guess which hole will shoot out hardest.
flow.say: When we pull off the tape, which hole do you think will squirt the hardest? The top, the middle or the bottom? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which hole will squirt hardest? Top, middle or bottom? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the bottom hole will squirt hardest?
good: Because it has the most water above it.
Because the water above pushes down on it.

flow.do: 1. Pull off the tape quickly. 2. Watch the three jets. 3. Keep watching as the bottle empties.
flow.say: Look at the three jets. Which one shoots out fastest? What happens to the jets as the water goes down?
flow.kid: Pull the tape off! Which jet is fastest? Watch as the water goes down.
flow.parent: The bottom jet shoots out fastest, and usually furthest, because the most water is above it. The top of the water has the furthest to fall to reach the bottom hole, and that fall gives the jet its speed. As the bottle empties, every jet gets weaker, because the water level is falling. The top jet stops first.

flow.do: Talk about the water tank on the roof, and the taps on each floor.
flow.say: Our building keeps water in a tank on the roof. Which tap do you think flows hardest, on the ground floor or the top floor? Why?
flow.kid: The tank is on the roof. Which tap flows hardest, ground floor or top floor? Why?

check.q: In a building with a tank on the roof, which tap usually flows hardest?
options: The tap on the top floor, nearest the tank
The tap on the ground floor, furthest below the tank
All taps flow the same
check.why: The ground-floor tap has the most water above it, so the water has fallen furthest when it reaches the tap. It comes out hardest, like the bottom hole of the bottle. Picking the top floor is a natural guess, because it is nearest the tank, but nearest is not what matters. Height above the tap is.

setup.caption: 1. Make three holes, one above the other, and tape them.

setup.art: The bottle full of water standing on an upturned steel bowl in a bucket, with three jets of water curving out, the lowest one fastest and furthest.
setup.caption: 2. Pull off the tape and watch the three jets.

activities.title: The Twirling Button
activities.context: In this activity you make an old toy from a button and a thread. The spinning button twists the thread, and the twisted thread spins the button back the other way.

materials.item: a big button with two or four holes, or a cardboard circle 5 cm across with two holes near the middle
strong thread or thin string, about 80 cm long

activities.safety: Keep the spinning button away from hair and faces.

schedule.what: Make the twirling button, get it spinning, and watch the thread twist and untwist.

activities.record: Draw the button and the twisted thread. Write where the energy waits when the button slows down and turns round.

flow.do: 1. Thread the string through two holes of the button. 2. Tie the ends to make a loop. 3. Slide the button to the middle. 4. Hold one end of the loop in each hand.
flow.say: This toy is very old. Children in India and in many other countries have played with it for hundreds of years. Let's thread it.
flow.kid: Thread the string through two holes. Tie the ends. Hold one end in each hand.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Twirling Button. You thread a button onto a loop of string.

flow.do: 1. Swing the button round in circles about 20 times, to twist the string. 2. Pull your hands apart. 3. Let your hands come closer as the string twists the other way. 4. Pull again.
flow.say: Twist it up first. Now pull, then let your hands come in, then pull again. Can you keep it spinning?
flow.kid: Swing it round to twist the string. Pull. Let your hands come in. Pull again!
flow.parent: It takes a few tries to find the rhythm. Pulling makes the button spin fast. As it spins, it twists the string the other way. When the button slows down, the twisted string holds the energy, and starts spinning the button back again.

flow.do: Ask your child to watch the moment the button stops and turns.
flow.say: Watch the button. At one moment it stops, and then it spins the other way. Where is the energy at that moment?
flow.kid: The button stops, then turns the other way. Where is the energy then?

check.q: When the twirling button stops for a moment, where is its energy?
options: It has all gone
In the twisted string
In your hands only
check.why: At the moment the button stops, the string is twisted tight, and the energy waits in the twist. Then the string untwists and spins the button again. Your pull adds a little more energy each time, to make up for what spreads out as sound and warmth.

projects.title: The Battery Diary: a week of watching a phone's store
projects.context: In this 5-day project you watch a phone's battery number every morning, afternoon and night. You find out how the store fills up and runs down, and what uses it fastest.

materials.item: a family phone that shows the battery level as a number
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Only a grown-up plugs the charger into the wall. Never touch a charger with wet hands.

schedule.what: Make the diary table. Write the battery number in the morning, the afternoon and at night. Write what the phone was used for.
Write the three numbers again. Note when the phone was charged.
Write the three numbers. Guess which use runs the battery down fastest.
Write the three numbers. Test your guess with a grown-up: 10 minutes of a video, then 10 minutes of the screen off.
Draw a line graph of the week. Say what fills the store and what empties it.

projects.record: A table with a row for each day and columns for morning, afternoon, night, and what the phone did. Then a line graph of the battery number over the week.

flow.do: 1. Rule a table in the notebook with 5 rows for 5 days. 2. Make columns for morning, afternoon, night and notes. 3. Read the battery number on the phone and write it in.
flow.say: A phone battery is a store of energy. Charging fills it, and using the phone empties it. Let's watch it for a week.
flow.kid: The phone battery is an energy store. Write its number three times a day.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 5-day project. You start a diary of a phone's battery number.

flow.wait: Come back each day for 3 more days.
flow.do: 1. Write the three numbers each day. 2. Write when the phone was charged, and what it was used for most.
flow.say: What is the number now? Was the phone charged? What was it used for today?
flow.kid: Write the number. Was it charged? What was it used for?

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, write the battery number. 2. Play a video for 10 minutes and write the number. 3. Leave the screen off for 10 minutes and write the number again.
flow.say: Which do you think empties the store faster, a video or the screen being off? Why? Let's test it.
flow.kid: Guess first. Video or screen off: which uses more? Why? Now test it.
flow.parent: A video with the screen bright usually takes a few percent in 10 minutes. With the screen off, the number usually stays the same or falls by 1. The screen and the speaker use the most energy.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line graph with the days along the bottom and the battery number up the side. 2. Look for where the line jumps up and where it falls fastest.
flow.say: Where does the line jump up? That is charging, when the store fills. Where does it fall fastest? What was the phone doing then?
flow.kid: Draw the line. Where does it go up? Where does it fall fastest?

check.q: In Kavya's battery diary, the number jumps from 20 to 100 overnight. What happened?
options: The phone made its own energy while it rested
The phone was charged, so energy from the wall was stored in its battery
The number was wrong
check.why: Charging pushes energy from the wall socket into the battery's chemicals, where it is stored. A phone cannot make its own energy. A battery only holds what it is given.

setup.caption: 1. Make the diary table and write the battery number.

setup.art: A hand-drawn line graph that falls during each day and jumps up each night, with small phone and plug drawings at the jumps.
setup.caption: 2. On day 5, draw the line graph of the week.

challenges.title: The Comeback Champion
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You change your roll-back jar to make it roll back as far as it can from just 3 turns.
challenges.problem: Change your roll-back jar so that, after exactly 3 turns, it rolls back further than before.
constraints: Use only things from home: jars, bands, weights, thread, tape.
materials: the roll-back jar from the experiment
extra rubber bands, thick and thin
different weights: a padlock, a nut, a stack of coins
a wider and a narrower jar, if you have them
general: Use two bands side by side instead of one, so the twist stores more energy.
Use a heavier weight, so the band can be twisted harder without the weight flipping over.
Use a wider jar, which rolls further in each turn.
creative: Put a rubber band round the outside of the jar like a tyre, and test whether it rolls further or less far.
Test the jar on a tiled floor, a mat and a bedsheet.
Make two jars and race them back to the start line.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own champion. Change one thing at a time, test it 3 times, and keep the change only if it helps.

flow.do: 1. Measure your jar's roll-back after 3 turns, three times. 2. Write the middle result. This is the number to beat.
flow.say: First let's find the number to beat. Three turns, three tries.
flow.kid: Wind 3 turns. Let go. Measure. Do it 3 times. That is your number to beat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Comeback Champion challenge. You find the distance to beat.

flow.do: 1. Choose one thing to change. 2. Test it 3 times. 3. Keep it only if the jar goes further. 4. Then try another change.
flow.say: Change only one thing at a time. If we change two things and it goes further, we won't know which one helped.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test it 3 times. Did it go further? Keep it or undo it.
flow.parent: Two bands side by side usually help, as long as the weight is heavy enough not to flip over. A wider jar rolls further in 3 turns, because each turn covers more floor. A soft mat makes the jar roll less far, because more energy spreads out into the mat.

flow.do: Show your best jar to the family, and explain why each change helped or did not help.
flow.say: Tell us what you changed, and why you think it helped.
flow.kid: Show your best jar. What did you change? Why did it help?

check.q: Meena, a girl in Class 4, changed two things at once, and her jar went further. What is the problem?
options: Nothing. It went further, so both changes helped
She cannot tell which change helped
She should have changed three things
check.why: With two changes at once, she cannot tell which one helped. One might have helped a lot and the other might even have made it worse. Changing one thing at a time is what makes a test fair.

setup.art: Three roll-back jars of different widths on a floor, with different bands and weights laid beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Gather jars, bands and weights to try.

setup.art: A child measuring a jar's roll-back with a tailor's tape along a floor, with a notebook of results beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Change one thing, test 3 times, measure.

challenges.title: The Slowest Marble
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You lift a marble up high and build a track on a cupboard door so that its stored energy carries it down as slowly as possible.
challenges.problem: Build a track on a cupboard door or a wall, from as high as you can reach down to the floor, so that a marble takes as long as possible to reach the bottom.
constraints: The marble must start at the top by itself, with no push.
It must keep moving all the way down, with no stops.
Use only paper, card, cardboard tubes and masking tape.
materials: cardboard tubes from kitchen rolls or toilet rolls, cut in half lengthwise
strips of thick card folded into channels
masking tape, which peels off without marking
general: Make a zigzag of gently sloping channels, so the marble goes back and forth across the door.
Make the slopes gentle, so the marble does not speed up much on each one.
creative: Add a funnel made from a paper cone, where the marble spirals round before dropping.
Add a short uphill part, where the marble uses some of its speed to climb.
Make a cup at the end that rings a steel bell or a spoon when the marble lands.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own slow track. Draw it first. Time it 3 times and try to beat your best.

flow.do: 1. Hold the marble at the top of the door and drop it straight down. 2. Time it.
flow.say: Up here, the marble has energy waiting, because it is high. If I just drop it, it all comes out in under a second. Can we make it take much longer?
flow.kid: Drop the marble from the top. Time it. Can we make it take longer?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slowest Marble challenge. You see how fast a marble falls straight down.

flow.do: 1. Tape channels in a zigzag down the door. 2. Test from the top after every two or three pieces. 3. Fix places where the marble jumps out or stops.
flow.say: Each channel must slope down a little. If it is too steep, the marble goes fast. If it is too flat, it stops.
flow.kid: Tape the channels in a zigzag. Each one slopes down a little. Test as you go.
flow.parent: Help with taping high up. Stand on the floor, not on a chair, unless a grown-up holds it. Slopes of about one finger-width drop for every 30 cm work well.

flow.do: 1. Time the marble 3 times. 2. Compare with the straight drop.
flow.say: The marble started at the same height both times, with the same energy waiting. Why did the track make it take so much longer?
flow.kid: Time it 3 times. Why does it take longer than the drop?

check.q: The marble starts at the same height for the straight drop and for the zigzag track. Which is true?
options: The track gives the marble more energy
The marble has the same energy waiting, but the track lets it out more slowly
The marble has no energy on the track
check.why: The marble starts at the same height, so the same energy is waiting. The gentle slopes let it come out a little at a time, so the marble never goes very fast. Some energy also spreads out as sound and warmth, as the marble rolls and bumps.

setup.caption: 1. Tape a zigzag track down a door.

setup.art: A child at the bottom of the door watching the marble roll along the last channel, holding a phone stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Let the marble go and time it.
