opts: Energy that is moving right now
Energy waiting in a thing, ready to come out later
Energy that has been used up
quiz.why: Stored energy waits until it is released. Picking 'used up' is a common mix-up: used energy has spread out, not stored.

quiz.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, holds a rubber band stretched between her fingers, without moving. Where is the energy?
opts: There is none, because nothing moves
In the stretch of the band
In the air around it
quiz.why: The stretch of the band holds the energy. It flies off when she lets go. Picking 'none' comes from thinking only moving things have energy.

quiz.p: In the roll-back jar, what does winding more turns do?
opts: Stores more energy in the twisted band, so the jar rolls back further
Makes the padlock lighter
Uses up the jar's energy
quiz.why: More turns mean more twist, and more twist holds more energy. That is why the jar rolled back further after 4 turns than after 1.

quiz.p: A roll-back jar is wound 3 turns and held still for a minute. What happens when it is let go?
opts: Nothing, because the energy leaked away
It rolls back about as far as without the wait
It rolls back much further, because it rested
quiz.why: The energy waited in the twisted band, so it still rolls back about as far. Waiting does not add energy, and in one minute the band loses only a tiny bit.

quiz.p: Why does a bouncing ball bounce lower each time, and stop in the end?
opts: The ball forgets how to bounce
Some energy spreads out as sound and warmth at each bounce
Gravity gets stronger
quiz.why: At each bounce some energy spreads out as sound and a little warmth in the ball and the floor. It cannot be collected again, so each bounce is lower.

quiz.p: Where does the water in the tank on the roof get the energy to flow to the taps?
opts: From its height, because a motor pumped it up there
From the taps
From the pipes
quiz.why: The motor lifted the water and stored energy in its height. When a tap is opened, the water falls and that energy comes out.

quiz.p: A coconut falls from a tall tree, and another falls from a short tree. Which hits the ground harder?
opts: The one from the short tree
The one from the tall tree
Both the same
quiz.why: The coconut higher up had more energy waiting, so it is moving faster when it lands. That is why you should never stand under a coconut palm.

quiz.p: Where did almost all the energy in a plate of ragi dosa first come from?
opts: The gas stove
Sunlight caught by the ragi plants
The water in the batter
quiz.why: Ragi plants caught sunlight and stored its energy in their grains. The stove only cooks the dosa. Picking the stove is a common guess, because the stove makes heat.

quiz.p: A biscuit packet says 'Energy 480 kcal per 100 g'. What does this tell you?
opts: How much energy is stored in 100 grams of the biscuits
How healthy the biscuits are
How many biscuits are in the packet
quiz.why: Kcal is a unit for the energy stored in food. The number tells you nothing about vitamins or protein.

quiz.p: Why can a tired cell that dims a torch often still run a wall clock?
opts: A clock needs only a tiny flow of electricity
A clock charges the cell
A clock uses no energy
quiz.why: A torch needs a big flow and a clock needs only a trickle. A tired cell can still push a trickle. A clock does use energy, just very little.

quiz.p: Which of these is a safe thing to do with an ordinary AA cell?
opts: Charge it in a phone charger
Put a tired one in a clock, and drop a finished one in e-waste
Open it to see the chemicals
quiz.why: Charging an ordinary cell can make it burst, and the chemicals inside can burn skin. Using it until it is finished, then giving it to e-waste, is safe.

quiz.p: Robert Mayer said that the warmth and movement of a body come from what?
opts: A special life force
The energy stored in food
The heat of the Sun on the skin
quiz.why: Mayer said a body's warmth and work come from the energy in food. Rubner's measurements with dogs later showed this. The 'life force' was the old idea he argued against.

items.p: Match each thing to where its energy is waiting.
pairs: Water in the tank on the roof
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the four kinds of store in this unit: height, shape, food and fuel, and cells. A strong answer can also say what would let each one out.

items.p: Energy that waits in a thing, ready to come out later, is called stored energy. Scientists also call it ____ energy.
items.why: Potential means 'able to happen later'. William Rankine gave stored energy this name in 1853.

items.p: Remember the roll-back jar, with a rubber band and a padlock inside. Why does the padlock need to hang from the middle of the band?
opts: To make the jar heavier so it rolls faster
To hold the middle of the band still, so rolling the jar twists the band
To make a noise as it rolls
items.why: The hanging padlock stays at the bottom while the jar turns, so the band's middle stays still and its ends twist. Without the weight, the whole band would just turn with the jar, and nothing would be stored. A heavier jar does not help it roll back.

items.p: A coconut hanging still on a high branch has no energy, because it is not moving.
items.why: False. The coconut has energy waiting in its height. If it falls, that energy becomes movement. Things that are still can hold stored energy.

items.p: In the roll-back jar test, you held the wound jar still for a minute, then let go. What happened, and what does it show about stored energy?
items.a: The jar still rolled back, about as far as without the wait. It shows that the energy stayed in the twisted band while the jar was held still, and came out when I let go.
items.why: A strong answer says what was seen and says where the energy waited: in the twist of the band.

items.p: Sort these into stores of energy and things where energy is moving.
items: a book on a high shelf
items.a: see items
items.why: Stores are things holding energy for later. Moving energy is energy being used right now as movement, light, heat or sound. A strong sorter asks: is something happening now?

items.p: Draw the roll-back jar as if you could see through it. Show the band, the padlock and the twist after 3 turns.
items.a: A jar on its side with a band from the middle of the base to the middle of the lid, a padlock hanging from the band's middle, and the band twisted on both sides of the padlock.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the padlock hanging down and the twist in the band on both sides of it. That twist is where the energy waits.
items.art: An empty outline of a jar lying on its side.

items.p: Nithya winds her roll-back jar 4 turns. Then she winds it 1 turn. Which time will it roll back further?
opts: After 1 turn
After 4 turns
The same both times
items.why: 4 turns twist the band more, so more energy waits in it, and the jar rolls back further. A strong answer gives that reason, not just the answer.

items.p: Which of these foods stores the most energy in every 100 grams?
opts: Cooking oil
Banana
Cucumber
items.why: Cooking oil stores about 900 kcal in every 100 grams. A banana has about 90, and a cucumber much less, because they are mostly water.

items.p: The energy in food, fuel and cells is stored in how their tiny particles are joined. It is called ____ energy.
items.why: Chemical energy comes out when a material changes, for example when gas burns or food is digested.

items.p: An ordinary AA cell can be charged again in a phone charger.
items.why: False. Only cells marked 'rechargeable' can be charged. Charging an ordinary cell can make it leak, get hot or burst.

items.p: Label the picture of a flat building with a water tank on the roof. Write 'most energy waiting' at the place where the water has furthest to fall, and 'tap that flows hardest' at the right tap.
items.a: 'Most energy waiting' goes on the tank, high on the roof. 'Tap that flows hardest' goes on the ground-floor tap, the furthest below the tank.
items.why: Water high up has the most energy waiting. The ground-floor tap has the most water above it, so it flows hardest.
items.art: A tall flat building with a tank on its roof, pipes running down, and a tap on the ground floor, the middle floor and the top floor.

items.p: Remember Ammamma's clock in the story, which stopped while she was away. Why did the clock stop, and what made it start again?
items.a: The clock stopped because nobody wound it, so its spring had let out all its stored energy. Ammamma wound the key, which coiled the spring tight and stored energy in it again.
items.why: A strong answer says nothing was broken: the store was empty, and winding filled it.

items.p: Remember the Tired Cell test, where a cell made a torch dim. Three people in a family in Kochi decide what to do with it.

views.says: Throw it in the e-waste bag. If it can't light a torch, it is finished.
Put it in the wall clock. It still has energy for something that needs only a little.
Keep it in a box for the remote. We may need it later.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use what you found in the Tired Cell test. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence, such as 'our tired cell ran the clock all night'. It then gives another side its due: an old cell left in a box for months can leak, so Amma is right that it should not be kept for ever.
items.why: There is a real trade-off. A tired cell still holds energy, but very old cells can leak, so using it soon is better than keeping it.

items.p: Put these in the order they happen when Ammamma's clock runs.
items: The spring slowly unwinds, one tick at a time
The spring is coiled tight, with energy waiting
After eight days the spring has no energy left
a: The spring is coiled tight, with energy waiting
The spring slowly unwinds, one tick at a time
After eight days the spring has no energy left
items.why: Energy goes in first, waits, comes out slowly, and then the store is empty.

items.p: Roshni, a girl in Class 3, says, 'My roll-back jar came back past the start line, so it got extra energy from somewhere.' What really happened?
opts: It got energy from the floor
It was moving fast at the start line, so it twisted the band the other way and kept going a little
The padlock pushed it
items.why: At the start line the band is untwisted, but the jar is moving fast. It keeps rolling and twists the band the other way, until it stops. It never gets more energy than was put in. It just changes between movement and twist.

items.p: Your roll-back jar never rolled back for ever. It rocked back and forth a few times and stopped. Where did its energy go?
items.a: Some energy spread out as a soft rumbling sound as the jar rolled on the floor. Some warmed the band a tiny bit as it twisted and untwisted, and some warmed the floor. That energy cannot be collected again, so the jar stopped.
items.why: A strong answer says the energy did not vanish. It spread out as sound and warmth.

items.p: Two friends in Madurai argue about a ball held high.

views.says: The stored energy is in the ball. The ball is the thing that falls.
The stored energy belongs to the ball and the Earth together, because it comes from the pull between them.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say what the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer might back Selvi: far from the Earth there is no pull, and lifting the ball would store almost nothing, so the Earth matters. It then gives Pavithra her due: it is the ball that speeds up, so saying the ball has the energy is a handy short way of talking.
items.why: Physicists say the energy belongs to the ball and the Earth together. Most people say it belongs to the ball, which is fine for everyday sums.

items.p: Sort these stores into how they let their energy out.
items: a phone battery during the day
items.a: see items
items.why: Some stores let everything out in a moment. Others let it out a little at a time. What matters is how the store is released, not how much it holds.

items.p: In the Three Holes test, which jet of water shot out hardest?
opts: The top hole
The middle hole
The bottom hole
items.why: The bottom hole had the most water above it. The top of the water had furthest to fall to reach that hole, so its jet was fastest.

items.p: As the bottle in the Three Holes test emptied, all three jets got weaker.
items.why: True. As the water level fell, every hole had less water above it, so every jet slowed. The top jet stopped first.

items.p: A flea must jump onto a passing dog, many times their own height. Their leg muscles are too slow to throw them that high. How does a flea solve this problem?
items.a: The flea slowly squeezes a pad of very springy material called resilin, and stores energy in it. Then they let it go all at once, so the jump is far quicker than their muscles alone could make it.
items.why: A strong answer says the energy is stored slowly and released fast. That is the flea's way of getting a big, quick jump from slow muscles.

items.p: Why does a seed carry a store of food?
opts: To feed birds
To grow a root and a shoot in the dark soil, before they have leaves to catch sunlight
To make the seed heavy so they fall
items.why: A young plant cannot make food until their first leaves reach the light. Until then, they live on the store their parent packed into the seed. Birds do eat seeds, but that is not what the store is for.

items.p: Almost all the energy in our food was first caught from ____ by plants.
items.why: Plants use sunlight to build sugar from air and water. Animals that eat plants, and people who eat both, get that stored sunlight energy.

items.p: Draw the Pop-Up Jumper folded flat with the band on the outside. Use an arrow to show which way the band pulls.
items.a: Two card squares folded together at the hinge, with the band running round the outside of the fold from notch to notch, and arrows showing the band pulling the cards to open flat.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the band stretched round the outside, because that is where it stores energy when the card is folded.

items.p: Why can a cell that is too tired for a torch often still run a wall clock?
opts: The clock makes its own electricity
The clock needs only a tiny flow of electricity, and a tired cell can still push that much
Clocks use a different kind of cell
items.why: A torch bulb needs a big flow of electricity. A clock needs only a trickle. A tired cell has some stored energy left, enough for the trickle.

items.p: Match each living thing to the store that helps their life.
pairs: fat in their hump, for days with little food
oil, to feed the young plant
a springy pad, for a huge jump
sugar in your muscles, for a sudden run
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each living thing stores energy in the way that solves their own problem.

items.p: Ishaan, a boy in Class 3, says, 'A toy that I wind up today and play with tomorrow will have more energy tomorrow, because it has rested.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. A store gives back only what was put in. Waiting does not add energy. The roll-back jar held still for a minute rolled back about as far as before, not further.
items.why: A strong answer uses the wait test as evidence.

items.p: Put these in order, from the food that stores the least energy in 100 grams to the one that stores the most.
items.why: Banana is about 90 kcal per 100 g, rice about 350, groundnuts about 570, and oil about 900. Foods with more fat store more energy, and foods with more water store less.

items.p: Label the parts of the roll-back jar: the band, the padlock, the twist, and the place where the energy waits.
items.a: The band runs from the lid to the base. The padlock hangs from its middle. The twist is in the band on both sides of the padlock. The energy waits in the twist.
items.why: A strong answer points to the twisted band, not the padlock or the jar, as the store.
items.art: A see-through drawing of a jar on its side with a twisted rubber band and a padlock inside, with four empty label lines.

items.p: A family in Hyderabad argues about the water tank on the roof.

views.says: The tank is a waste. The motor uses electricity to pump water up, so why not pump it straight to the taps?
The tank is useful. The motor runs once, and then the water flows to the taps by itself, any time, even in a power cut.
The tank is useful, but the top floor gets weak water. Put it higher.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Use what you know about water stored high up. Then answer back from one of the other views.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the tank is a store of energy: the motor puts energy in once, and the water can come out later, even in a power cut. It also gives Farzana her due, since pumping and storing take some electricity, and Dadi hers, since a higher tank does give more push to every tap.
items.why: Each view has something right. A store costs energy to fill, but it lets the energy come out later, when it is needed.

items.p: Ammamma winds her clock for a few minutes, and it ticks for eight days. Does the clock get more energy out than Ammamma put in? Explain.
items.a: No. The clock lets the energy out very slowly, a tiny bit at each tick, so a few minutes of winding last eight days. But the total energy out is no more than went in. Some of it even spreads out as sound and warmth.
items.why: A strong answer separates how long a store lasts from how much it holds.

items.p: Durga winds her roll-back jar 10 turns, much more than before. The padlock flips over inside, and the jar does not roll back at all. Why?
opts: 10 turns removed all the energy
The twist pulled so hard that it swung the padlock over, so the band unwound inside instead of turning the jar
The jar was too heavy
items.why: With too many turns, the band pulls harder than the padlock's weight can resist. The padlock swings up and over, and the band unwinds without turning the jar. A heavier weight would let her wind more turns.

items.p: Mayer saw that sailors' blood was bright red in hot Java and dark in cold Germany. Explain how this led him to the idea that body heat comes from food.
items.a: He thought the body burns food slowly with oxygen to keep warm. In a hot place the body needs less warmth, so it uses less oxygen from the blood, and the blood stays bright red. So warmth must come from burning food, not from a special life force.
items.why: A strong answer joins the colour of the blood to the use of oxygen, and the oxygen to burning food for warmth.

items.p: Max Rubner kept dogs in a closed box and measured all the heat they gave out. What did his result show?
opts: Dogs make heat from nothing
The heat matched the energy in the food the dogs used
Dogs give out more heat than their food holds
items.why: The heat matched the energy in the food almost exactly. That showed living bodies follow the same rule as everything else: energy is not made from nothing.

items.p: Draw a comic strip in four boxes: energy going into a store, waiting, and coming out later. Use any store from this unit.
items.a: For example: 1. A child rolls the jar 3 turns. 2. The child holds it still and counts to 60. 3. The child lets go. 4. The jar rolls back. Each box has a label: in, waiting, out.
items.why: A strong strip shows all three stages, including the waiting, which is the heart of a store.
items.art: Four empty comic boxes in a row.

items.p: Two jars are wound 3 turns each. One is held still for a minute before letting go, the other is let go at once. The held jar rolls back about the same distance.
items.why: True. The energy waits in the twisted band. A rubber band loses only a very small part of it in a minute.

items.p: The Mettur dam on the Kaveri river holds a huge lake of water high up behind it. Explain how the dam stores energy, and how that energy reaches a fan in a home in Chennai.
items.a: The water behind the dam is high up, so energy waits in its height. When the gates open, the water falls through pipes and spins machines that make electricity. The electricity travels along wires to Chennai, where it turns a fan.
items.why: A strong answer names the store (height), the release (the fall), and the journey of the energy.

items.p: Sort these into stores that can be filled again and stores that cannot be filled again.
items.a: see items
items.why: Some stores can be filled again by putting energy back in, such as charging, winding or pumping. When a fuel burns or an ordinary cell's chemicals are used up, the material has changed, and it cannot be filled again at home.

items.p: Coal is a store of energy from plants that lived millions of years ago. Where did those plants get the energy?
opts: From the Earth's heat
From sunlight
From the coal
items.why: Those plants caught sunlight, like plants today. Their bodies were buried and slowly turned into coal. So coal stores very old sunlight.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether a thick rubber band or a thin one stores more energy in the roll-back jar. Say what you change, what you keep the same, and what you measure.
items.a: Change only the band: thick, then thin. Keep the same jar, padlock, floor and number of turns, for example 3. Measure how far the jar rolls back, 3 times for each band, and use the middle result.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and repeats each try.

items.p: The scientist who first gave stored energy the name potential energy, in 1853, was William ____.
items.why: William Rankine was a Scottish engineer who worked on steam engines.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: said body heat comes from the energy in food
measured the heat of dogs and matched it to their food
said nobody knows what energy really is
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of them added a piece to what we know about stored energy, and what we do not know.

items.p: Label the twirling button picture at the moment the button stops: where the energy is waiting, and which way the button will turn next.
items.a: The energy is waiting in the tightly twisted string on both sides of the button. The button will turn the opposite way to how it was spinning before.
items.why: A strong answer points to the twisted string, and sees that the untwisting turns the button back.
items.art: A button on a string loop between two hands, the string tightly twisted, the button still.

items.p: A bow stores energy slowly and gives it out in a moment. A clock stores it quickly and gives it out slowly. Name one other store of each kind, and say why it is useful that way.
items.a: Slow in, fast out: a flea's springy pad, because a quick release gives a big jump. Fast in, slow out: a phone battery, charged in two hours and used all day, because we need a little energy for a long time.
items.why: A strong answer gives a correct example of each and says how the timing helps.

applications: Wind-up clocks and watches store energy in a coiled spring.
Water tanks on roofs store energy in height, so taps work without a pump running.
Hydroelectric power stations, such as those at Mettur and Idukki, store water high behind dams.
Phones, laptops, electric scooters and inverters store energy in rechargeable batteries.
Bows, catapults and trampolines store energy in a bent or stretched shape.
Food packets print the energy stored in the food, in kcal.
Pull-back toy cars store energy in a spring when they are pulled back.
Clothes pegs, hair clips and stapler springs hold things by pressing with stored energy.
Cars and buses carry stores of energy as petrol, diesel, gas or batteries.

open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure it very exactly and the numbers always add up, but nobody can say what it is made of.

open_questions.q: Can we build batteries that store much more energy, cheaply and safely, to keep solar electricity for the night?
open_questions.why_open: Many teams are working on new kinds of batteries, but none yet is cheap, safe, long-lasting and able to hold a lot.

open_questions.q: Is the total energy of the whole universe exactly zero?
open_questions.why_open: Some physicists think the stored energy of gravity might exactly balance all the other energy. Nobody knows how to check this.

open_questions.q: How do some seeds stay alive while they wait for years, even hundreds of years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some ways seeds protect themselves while dry, but not why some kinds can wait so much longer than others.

maths.problem: Remember the roll-back jar, wound 1, 2, 3 and 4 turns. Divya's middle results were 40 cm, 75 cm, 105 cm and 130 cm. How much further did each extra turn send the jar? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 35 cm, then 30 cm, then 25 cm. Each extra turn adds a little less than the one before.
maths.explain: 75 - 40 = 35. 105 - 75 = 30. 130 - 105 = 25. The gaps get 5 cm smaller each time. So more turns always help, but each extra turn helps a little less.
maths.context: This is about the Roll-Back Jar experiment, where you wind a jar a number of turns and measure how far it rolls back.
maths.why_maths: Finding the gaps between results shows a pattern you cannot see from the numbers alone.

maths.problem: Using Divya's pattern, where each extra turn adds 5 cm less than the one before, predict how far her jar would roll back after 5 turns.
maths.explain: The last gap was 25 cm. The next gap should be 5 cm less, which is 20 cm. 130 + 20 = 150 cm. This is only a prediction. With too many turns the padlock may flip over, so the test must check it.
maths.context: This is about the Roll-Back Jar experiment, using Divya's results for 1 to 4 turns.
maths.why_maths: A number pattern lets you make a prediction, and then a test can show whether the pattern holds.

maths.problem: Ammamma turns the key of her clock 10 times every Sunday. How many turns does she make in 4 weeks? In a year of 52 weeks?
maths.answer: 40 turns in 4 weeks. 520 turns in a year.
maths.explain: 4 lots of 10 is 40. 52 lots of 10 is 520. All the clock's ticking for a whole year comes from those 520 turns of the key.
maths.context: This is about Ammamma's eight-day clock in the story, which she winds every Sunday.
maths.why_maths: Counting equal groups shows how a small amount of winding each week adds up to all the energy for a year.

maths.problem: In Kavya's battery diary, the phone showed 100% at 7 in the morning and 60% at 3 in the afternoon. How much did it drop each hour, if it dropped the same amount each hour? At that rate, at what time will it reach 20%?
maths.answer: 5% each hour. It will reach 20% at 11 at night.
maths.explain: From 7 to 3 is 8 hours. 100 - 60 = 40. 40 shared over 8 hours is 5 each hour. From 60 to 20 is 40 more, which takes another 8 hours. 3 in the afternoon plus 8 hours is 11 at night.
maths.context: This is about the Battery Diary project, where you write down a phone's battery number through the day.
maths.why_maths: Sharing the drop over the hours shows how fast the store empties, so you can predict when it will need charging.

maths.problem: 100 grams of cooking oil stores about 900 kcal. 100 grams of banana stores about 90 kcal. How many times as much energy does the oil store? How many grams of banana hold as much energy as 100 grams of oil?
maths.answer: 10 times as much. 1,000 grams, which is 1 kilogram, of banana.
maths.explain: 900 is 10 lots of 90. So oil stores 10 times as much for its weight. To match it you need 10 lots of 100 grams of banana, which is 1,000 grams. A banana is mostly water, which stores no energy.
maths.context: This is about the food packet activity, where you read the energy number on food packets.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers shows how different foods are as stores of energy, which a list alone does not make clear.

roots.context: We have wound a jar, tested a tired cell and found energy waiting all over the house. Now we ask what a store of energy tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You wound the jar, held it still for a minute, then let go, and it rolled back. Your push had ended a minute before the rolling began. In between, the energy waited in the twisted band. So a store lets the energy of a push given now come out later, quickly or slowly.
deep_truth.habit: We expect a cause and its effect to happen together: the push, then straight away the movement. A store breaks that link in time. The cause can end long before the effect begins, like Ammamma's Sunday winding and Thursday's ticking.
deep_truth.evidence: In the wait test of the Roll-Back Jar, the jar held still for a minute still rolled back about as far as before. In the story, ten turns of a key kept a clock ticking for eight days.

three.who_am_i: You are a store too. Today's lunch waits in your body as the energy for this evening's run.
three.what_is_life: A seed holds food from their parent plant, sometimes for years, until water tells them it is time to grow.
three.what_is_this_world: Water held high behind a dam waits in the hills, until the gates open and it lights a city.

roots.thread: Before you wind the jar, the band is loose and nothing is waiting in it. Winding gathers your pushes into one store. Let go, and that one store comes out as many things: rolling, a soft rumble, and a little warmth in the band and the floor. The same store could have spun a wheel or lifted a weight instead. One store of energy can become many different happenings.

teachings.teaching: When it is time to wait, be still like a heron. When the moment comes, strike as quickly as the heron.
teachings.link: A heron standing still in the water is not idle. She is ready. Your wound jar held still in your hand was ready in the same way, and moved the moment you let go.

teachings.teaching: Aristotle said a thing can be something 'in potential' before it is that thing 'in action'. A builder who is resting can still build. Our word energy comes from his Greek word energeia, which means being at work.
teachings.link: The scientists' word for stored energy, potential energy, comes from the same old idea. A wound band is rolling in potential, until you let go and it rolls in action.

teachings.teaching: A tree too big to hug grows from a tiny shoot. A tower nine storeys high begins with a heap of earth. A journey of a thousand miles begins under your feet.
teachings.link: Big happenings often begin long before we see them. A week of ticking began with a few turns of a key, and a run in the evening began at lunch.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed. A store can give back only what was put into it, and some of that always spreads out as warmth.
The energy stored by lifting a thing belongs to the thing and the Earth together, because it comes from the pull between them.
What energy actually is, beyond the numbers that measure it, is still argued about.

other_view.view: Stored energy is a number we calculate to make our sums come out right. Nothing is really 'waiting' in a band. There are only atoms pushed out of place, pushing back. Saying it waits, like a heron, is a picture, not a finding.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Choices made: the main investigation is the roll-back jar, because it shows energy waiting where a child can hold it, and its result can be measured with a tailor's tape on any flat floor. A clear plastic jar is used rather than a tin, because a grown-up can pierce plastic with a nail and the child can see the twist. The padlock must hang without touching the side. If it flips over inside, the steps say to use a heavier weight or fewer turns. The jar may roll past the start line and rock back, so the steps say to measure only to where it first stops. Four turns of a 10 cm jar need about 1.3 metres of floor each side, which a hall or corridor gives. The Tired Cell test may find a cell that is fully flat, so it suggests testing a second one. Food energy is read from packets, not measured by burning food, so no flame is needed. The three-holes bottle is done over a bucket in the bathroom. The spine is the intro, the home hunt, the roll-back jar, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1840 Julius Robert Mayer, a young German doctor, sailed on a Dutch ship to Java, an island in what is now Indonesia. Doctors then often let a little blood out of sick people. In the hot harbour, Mayer saw that blood from the sailors' veins was bright red. In cold Germany it was dark. Mayer worked out a reason. The body burns food slowly with oxygen to keep warm. In a hot place it needs less warmth, so it uses less of the oxygen in the blood, and the blood stays bright. Many scientists then thought a special life force made a body's heat and movement. Mayer said the warmth and work of a body come from the energy stored in food, and energy is never made from nothing. A science journal would not print his first paper. He published another in 1842, and few people listened. Later scientists tested the idea. In the 1890s Max Rubner, a German scientist, kept dogs in a closed box and measured all the heat they gave out. It matched the energy in the food they had used, almost exactly.
how_we_found_out.who: Julius Robert Mayer, a German ship's doctor, and later Max Rubner, a German scientist
how_we_found_out.when: 1840 (the voyage to Java), 1842 (Mayer's paper) and 1894 (Rubner's measurements with dogs)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought a special life force made a body's heat and movement, apart from food. Mayer argued that both come from the energy stored in food. Rubner's measurements showed the heat a dog gives out matches the energy in their food.
